title: Product photography for a food brand
metaTitle: Photography for a food brand's shelf
excerpt: Photograph the pack and an honest serving under one light and one crop. Mixed backgrounds make a small food line look like a sampler.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. Food photography is a flow: the pack, the serving, the same light every time.
caption: A flow on paper: pack, serving, same light. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What two photographs does a packaged food need?
faqs.answer: A pack hero that matches the rest of the line, and a taste frame of an honest serving. The pack is what the grid shrinks. The dish proves what the food becomes. A garnish you do not sell, or a pile that misrepresents the weight, will read as a different product.

faqs.question: Should ingredients be written on the photo?
faqs.answer: Put them in the page as text, and let alt text describe the jar and the view. Required label text should still be readable in the pack frame, but a JPEG is a bad place to keep the only copy of an allergen. When the recipe changes, the text and the label photo both have to change.

faqs.question: How do you keep a small food line looking like one brand?
faqs.answer: One background, one camera height per format, and the same margin so a tin looks larger than a jar because it is. Shoot the line in one light. Marble one week and linen the next is how a careful kitchen starts to look like a sampler.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A food brand product photography practice has to make taste visible through the pack and the prepared food, under one crop and one light. The buyer cannot smell the jar. Mixed backgrounds will make a small line look like a sampler of other companies.

Photograph the pack as the object you ship, and the dish as proof of what it becomes. Keep those two jobs distinct so the grid stays a brand.

## Two frames, two jobs

Every product needs a pack hero and a taste frame. The pack hero is what the collection page shrinks: label readable, shape recognizable, background shared with the rest of the line. The taste frame shows the food as eaten, in the same light family, without becoming a different brand's cookbook.

- Pack, front, margins matched to the other products.
- Pack, three-quarter, if the shape is part of the product, such as a bottle or a tin.
- Prepared food, one honest serving, with a utensil or a hand only if it explains use.
- An ingredient scatter only when the ingredients are the story and they match the list on the page.

If the label has required text, the pack frame must not crop it into unreadability, and the page must still carry ingredients as text. A photograph of a label is not a substitute for the allergen list. The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) asks for text alternatives and for text that is actually text. Alt for the hero can be "Glass jar of chili crisp, black lid, front label visible." The ingredients live in the page. The W3C principles, including perceivable and understandable, fail when the only copy of an allergen is a blurry JPEG.

Do not burn "best seller" or a price into the file. You will change both, and the file will lie.

## Light that makes food look like food

Appetite is mostly light and moisture. A single soft source from the side, a white card for fill, and a background quieter than the food will beat a complicated set you cannot repeat. Shoot the line in one session if you can. Jars shot months apart under different warmth will look like different recipes.

Watch the highlights on glass and oil. A clipped highlight on a bottle erases the liquid's color, which is the taste cue. Expose for the food. Let the background go a little darker rather than blowing the chili oil into orange plastic.

Steam, melt, and herbs wilt. Shoot the prepared plate when it looks the way you would serve it to a guest, not ten minutes later when you have adjusted a light. If you need ten minutes, remake the plate. Publishing a tired dish and calling it rustic is how the brand drifts from the kitchen.

Color match matters more here than in many categories because people use color as a flavor. A ketchup-red that is actually your darker sauce will create the wrong expectation. Compare the file to the jar in daylight, on a phone, before you approve it. You cannot control their screen. You can refuse the worst grade.

## One background, or the shelf falls apart

Pick the background the pack can sit on for a year. Paper, a painted board, a single table. Use it for every hero. A marble week, a linen week, and a beach week in one collection is the unfinished grid. Lifestyle images can exist on the homepage. They should not be the thumbnail unless the whole system is lifestyle, and even then the crop and the horizon have to match.

Set the camera height and distance per format. Bottles share a height. Pouches share a height. Jars share a height. Do not shoot one jar from above and the next from the side and expect the category to look intended. Overhead can be the system for a line of flat bags. It is a poor surprise in a line of bottles.

Scale lies when you fill the frame with a small jar and then fill it again with a large tin. Leave the same margin. The tin should look larger because it is larger. That is the point of a consistent crop. A buyer choosing a gift will use the grid as a size comparison whether you meant them to or not.

Groups and hampers get their own frame, pulled back until every included product is visible. A hero that hides one jar will produce "where is the honey?" messages. If the hamper is the product, the hamper is the hero, and the single jars keep theirs.

## Files, speed, and the page jumping

Food images are the largest paint on the page. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) asks for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Export the size the template uses. Reserve the ratio so the ingredients do not jump down when the jar arrives. A jump next to an add-to-cart control is how people order the wrong item.

Name files by product and view: crisp-pack-front, crisp-eggs. The person who updates a seasonal label should be able to replace one frame without guessing. When the label changes, the photograph changes. An old label on a new recipe is a false ingredient list told in pictures.

Keep masters. The next template will want a different crop, and recropping a small export will cut off the lid or the margin you set. The direction sheet includes the master, the export, and the alt pattern.

Retouch crumbs that are accidents. Do not retouch the food into a gloss it does not have. Oil that is shiny in life can be shiny in the file. Oil that has been painted on in software will look like a different product beside the honest pack shot, and the seam will show in the gallery.

## What to stop putting in the frame

Stop adding garnishes you do not sell and the recipe does not use. A lime on the rim of a drink you do not include will show up as a complaint, or as a misunderstanding of the taste. If the garnish is essential to how you want it eaten, say so in the method, and consider whether it belongs.

Stop using hands with manicures, watches, and sleeves that change every product. If a hand explains scale or use, use one consistent approach: a simple spoon, or a hand with a plain cuff, every time. Inconsistent styling is a mixed crop even when the camera never moved.

Stop shooting "abundance" piles that misrepresent the weight in the jar. A frame full of chili flakes beside a small jar tells a generous story the scale does not. Show the serving you mean. The net weight is in text, and the picture should not contradict it.

If a product melts, do not shoot it in a state you cannot ship. A draped, softened bar may be honest, but then the page must say it melts and the photograph is not a defect. If you need it solid, shoot it solid, and do not leave it under the light until it slumps.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include the shop and the art direction around a catalog like this. The useful session is one background, a pack frame, a taste frame, and exports that will not blow the page apart.

## Cold food, hot food, and the clock

Some dishes cannot wait for a styling conversation. Broth, ice cream, and anything with a melt or a skin need the shot list finished before you cook. Set the camera, the distance, and the plate. Then cook. If the first frame fails, you are remaking the dish, not nudging a light for twenty minutes while the surface dies. Put that rule on the call sheet so a photographer who is new to the kitchen does not treat a melting subject like a jar.

Frozen and chilled products that must look cold can be shot cold, with the condensation you actually get, not a spray that reads as rain. If condensation obscures the label, shoot the pack hero dry and the taste frame cold. They are different jobs. A single frame that tries to be both will blur the brand name, and the grid will suffer.

Hot oil and sugar move. Decide the moment, such as the pour or the settled spoon, and repeat that moment for every product in the family. One sauce mid-pour and the next fully plated is a mixed crop of time. The line should look like it was served by the same cook.

## A direction page the kitchen can follow

Write the rules on one page: background, camera height per format, the frame set, the export, the alt pattern, and the rule that ingredients are text. The cook and the photographer may be different people. The page is how the brand survives that.

When you add a format, such as a tin after a line of jars, add a row to the direction before the shoot. Do not discover the crop while the oven is on. Revisit the page when the label design changes, because a new label may need more margin to stay readable at thumbnail size. Test that thumbnail in the real category template, on a phone, before you cook the next batch of hero dishes.

Rejects get a reason: clipped oil, wrong height, garnish, tired plate. Next time you will not relitigate them. The grid is the approval, not the single frame that looked delicious on the camera back.

Furniture is the next object that refuses to be a thumbnail. [An online shop for a furniture maker](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-furniture-maker) is the piece that follows, because scale, material, and lead time have to be on the page before anyone pays for something that will occupy a room.
